en: Now, what about functions that take 2
arguments? For example, take this login
function here.
It takes an email and a password and then
internally it might be doing whatever logic
is required to log a user in, to create a
session for the user, for example.
This again is something which
makes sense and which is expected. Here we
have 2 parameters but the order is not
surprising because in most forms we also
have the email field first and the password
field second.
So this order of arguments makes sense. And
calling this function is very readable. It's
immediately obvious what this function does
and that we have an email address and a
password as expected parameters. So this
could be an example for a 2-argument
function, which is no problem at all.
Another example would be this Point class,
which we instantiate by using the Point
constructor. We take 2 arguments here, the x
and the y coordinate, and this again is
really just common sense. It is expected
that the x argument is the first argument
and the y value is the second parameter, and
therefore this is easy to understand, easy
to read, and does nothing unexpected.
We don't need to think a lot about calling
this constructor function here because it is
very obvious what it does and what these
values will be.
So as you can probably tell by now,
it is about minimizing the number of
parameters,
but it's simply also about how
readable and how easy to understand a

If it's obvious which parameters it needs
and in which order these parameters need to
be provided, like in this login or point

Because after all,

For example, here a better solution could be
to split this one function into 2 functions
where one function is dedicated to normal
messages and one function focuses on errors.
That way we have 2 functions with one
argument each which then again are way
easier to call and understand. And that is
what clean code is all about, questioning
the code you have and trying to always
improve it such that it's more readable,
easier to understand, and requires less
thinking and reasoning about the code.
